Missing value patterns across the portfolio.




Four variables contain missing values. fuel_type (1,287 missing, 0.36%) and vehicle_value (513 missing, 0.14%) account for nearly all of it. The remaining columns have two or fewer NAs each. Because missingness is concentrated in non-target descriptive variables and represents under half a percent of records, listwise deletion is acceptable without introducing meaningful selection bias.
Before applying listwise deletion, the records flagged for removal are profiled against the records to be retained, to verify that deletion does not introduce systematic bias.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
2.4 Variable encoding
Categorical variables are imported as character vectors. Converting them to factors with explicit, meaningful level ordering improves both downstream plot readability and statistical test behaviour.
Two ordering choices warrant explanation. The policy_type levels are ordered from least to most comprehensive coverage (TP, TPG, CC, COMP_E, COMP_N), enabling monotonic interpretation of loss-ratio gradients across coverage tiers. The bonus_score levels are ordered from best to worst claim history (G, N, B), following the bonus-malus convention used by motor insurers.


Show the code
clean <- raw |>
  mutate(
    year             = as.integer(year),
    policy_type      = factor(policy_type,
                              levels = c("TP","TPG","CC","COMP_E","COMP_N")),
    policy_status    = factor(policy_status, levels = c("A","C"),
                              labels = c("Active","Cancelled")),
    business_type    = factor(business_type, levels = c("NB","P"),
                              labels = c("New business","Persistent")),
    payment_frequency = factor(payment_frequency, levels = c("A","S","Q"),
                               labels = c("Annual","Semi-annual","Quarterly")),
    bonus_score      = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("G","N","B"),
                              labels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad")),
    fuel_type        = factor(fuel_type, levels = c("D","G"),
                              labels = c("Diesel","Gasoline")),
    municipality_type = factor(municipality_type, levels = c("I","C","IS"),
                               labels = c("Interior","Coastal","Islands")),
    circulation_area = factor(circulation_area, levels = c("U","R"),
                              labels = c("Urban","Rural"))

Most checks return zero, indicating no out-of-range or logically inconsistent values across age, premium, and claim-count variables. Two findings warrant comment:

49 policy-years (0.01%) have zero exposure, representing policies that did not go on risk during their observation year, most likely from same-day cancellations or administrative records with immediately-closed exposure windows. The derived claim_frequency variable is computed conditionally on total_exposure > 0, returning NA for these records, so they do not distort downstream frequency calculations.
8,498 policy-years (2.4%) have a recorded claim count but zero incurred losses. This is a known pattern in motor insurance data, arising from claims that are opened and later closed at zero cost (denial, withdrawal, or below-deductible settlement) or claims still open at the year-end extraction. These records are retained: they contribute to claim frequency but not to incurred losses, which is the appropriate treatment.

total_exposure is bounded above by 1 in all 352,340 records, confirming the variable’s intended semantics as the fraction of the policy-year on risk. A second consistency check verifies that the seven coverage-specific premium and claim columns sum exactly to total_premium and total_claims. Any mismatch would indicate a data assembly error in the source file.


Show the code

  summarise(
    claims_sum_mismatch = sum(
      abs(total_claims - (liability_claims + property_claims + theft_claims +

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
2.6 Derived analytical variables
The brief identifies portfolio profitability and volatility as the outcomes of interest, but neither exists in the raw data. Both must be derived from the relationship between premiums collected, losses incurred, and policy exposure. Three policy-level metrics form the foundation:

Loss ratio: incurred losses divided by earned premium. The industry-standard measure of pure underwriting profitability before expense loading. A loss ratio below approximately 70% indicates a contribution to operating profit on a motor book.
Claim frequency: claim count divided by exposure (in policy-years). Exposure-normalising is essential because most policies in this dataset are on-risk for only part of the year (mean exposure 0.71).
Claim severity: incurred losses divided by claim count, defined only where claims occurred.



Show the code
clean <- clean |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio      = if_else(total_premium > 0,
                              total_incurred / total_premium, NA_real_),
    claim_frequency = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                              total_claims / total_exposure, NA_real_),
    claim_severity  = if_else(total_claims > 0,
                              total_incurred / total_claims, NA_real_)
  )


Three additional banded variables are constructed to support bivariate segmentation. Bands use breaks informed by the underlying distributions (verified in Section 3) and motor underwriting practice.


Show the code
clean <- clean |> 
  mutate(
    driver_age_band = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(0, 25, 35, 50, 65, Inf),
                          labels = c("<25","25-34","35-49","50-64","65+"),
                          right = FALSE),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(vehicle_age,
                           breaks = c(-1, 2, 5, 10, 15, Inf),
                           labels = c("0-2","3-5","6-10","11-15","16+"),
                           right = TRUE),
    vehicle_value_band = cut(vehicle_value,
                             breaks = quantile(vehicle_value,
                                               probs = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1),
                                               na.rm = TRUE),
                             labels = c("Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4"),
                             include.lowest = TRUE)
  )


The band cutoffs are reported below for transparency. Driver-age and vehicle-age bands use hardcoded breaks aligned with actuarial convention and depreciation milestones respectively; vehicle-value bands are computed as quartiles of the observed distribution.


Show the code
bind_rows(
  tibble(
    variable = "driver_age_band",
    breaks = "0 / 25 / 35 / 50 / 65 / Inf",
    rationale = "Actuarial convention: <25 is the conventional high-risk band; 65+ is the standard senior threshold"
  ),
  tibble(
    variable = "vehicle_age_band",
    breaks = "0 / 3 / 6 / 11 / 16 / Inf",
    rationale = "Aligned with depreciation and warranty milestones"
  ),
  tibble(
    variable = "vehicle_value_band",
    breaks = paste(round(quantile(clean$vehicle_value,
                                   probs = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1),
                                   na.rm = TRUE)), collapse = " / "),
    rationale = "Quartiles of the observed distribution; vehicle value spans several orders of magnitude"
  )
) |>
  kable(caption = "Band definitions used for downstream segmentation")

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
2.7 Volatility metric
Volatility is operationalised at the segment level as the coefficient of variation (CV) of loss ratio across the policies within a segment. Unlike standard deviation, CV is scale-free, making it directly comparable across segments with very different loss-ratio means. A high CV indicates that a segment’s profitability is unstable. Even if its mean loss ratio is acceptable, the distribution of individual-policy outcomes is wide, raising the risk of unexpected losses in any given year.
This summary is computed on demand within the bivariate analysis (Section 4) rather than added to the policy-level data frame, as it is inherently a group-level statistic.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3.1 Methodology
Univariate analysis serves two purposes in this exercise. First, it documents the shape of each variable, including central tendency, spread, skewness, and modality, which constrains the techniques available for bivariate analysis. Second, it surfaces concentrations and outliers that often turn out to be the loss drivers the brief asks the analyst to identify.
Two visual conventions are used:

Continuous variables: a histogram paired with a horizontal boxplot via the patchwork package. The histogram shows distribution shape. The boxplot makes outliers and the five-number summary explicit. The composite is a more honest representation than either alone.
Categorical variables: an ordered bar chart with frequency labels. Ordering by frequency (rather than alphabetical or factor-default) reveals concentration immediately, with the most common category at the top.



Show the code
clean <- read_rds("Data/motor_clean.rds")

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3.2 Continuous variables

3.2.1 Driver age


Show the code
h_age <- ggplot(clean, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of policies") +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

b_age <- ggplot(clean, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "grey30",
               width = 0.5, outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Driver age (years)", y = NULL) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

(h_age / b_age + plot_layout(heights = c(4, 1))) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Driver age ranges from 22 to 82, centred in mid-40s",
    subtitle = "Distribution of driver age across 352,340 policy-years",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10,
                                   margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey50", size = 8, hjust = 0)
    )
  )









The driver-age distribution spans 22 to 82 years, centred in the mid-40s, with a modest right tail of older drivers. The under-25 segment is small in volume but structurally important: it is the conventional high-risk pool in motor underwriting and becomes a focal point of the bivariate analysis. The 65+ tail is similarly relevant, as senior drivers carry distinct accident-risk profiles.

b_va <- ggplot(clean, aes(x = vehicle_age)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "grey30",

(h_va / b_va + plot_layout(heights = c(4, 1))) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Most insured vehicles are between 18 and 36 years old",
    subtitle = "Distribution of vehicle age across 352,340 policy-years",

The vehicle-age distribution spans 0 to about 60 years, with most vehicles concentrated between 18 and 36 years old (the IQR) and a median around 25 years. This is an unusually aged portfolio: the bulk of insured vehicles are over 15 years old, with a long tail of vehicles older than 40. The shape suggests two underwriting considerations. Theft exposure tends to concentrate in newer, higher-value vehicles, of which this portfolio has few. Breakdown and mechanical-failure claims rise with vehicle age, which this portfolio has in abundance. These tensions surface in the bivariate analysis of coverage tier and in the driver-age × vehicle-age risk surface.

  geom_bar(fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white") +
  geom_text(stat = "count",
            aes(label = comma(after_stat(count))),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "97% of policy-years are in the Good bonus-malus category",
    subtitle = "Distribution of bonus-malus category across 352,340 policy-years",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of policies",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data)."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11)









The bonus-malus distribution is extreme: 96.5% of policy-years sit in the Good category, with Neutral (2.2%) and Bad (1.3%) together accounting for the remaining 3.5%. The two smaller categories are sufficient in absolute volume for statistical testing (several thousand records each) but small in relative terms. This imbalance becomes important in Section 4.4, where the analysis shows that the small Neutral pool carries a disproportionate share of the portfolio’s loss-ratio deterioration.


3.3.3 Other categoricals


Show the code
cat_vars <- c("policy_status", "business_type", "payment_frequency",
              "fuel_type", "municipality_type", "circulation_area")

cat_summary <- clean |>
  select(all_of(cat_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  count(variable, value) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable,
                            levels = cat_vars,
                            labels = c("Policy status",
                                       "Business type",
                                       "Payment frequency",
                                       "Fuel type",
                                       "Municipality type",
                                       "Circulation area")))

ggplot(cat_summary, aes(x = fct_reorder(value, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 2.8, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Most categorical variables are heavily concentrated in their dominant category",
    subtitle = "Distribution of six categorical variables across 352,340 policy-years",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of policies",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nPercentages are within-variable; bars within each facet are sorted by frequency."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey20", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", colour = NA),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines")
  )









Several concentrations are worth noting. The portfolio is predominantly new business (69%) rather than persistent renewals (31%), pointing to rapid book growth across the period. New business typically carries higher loss ratios than renewals because insurers price renewals more precisely from claims history, so a fast-growing book can deteriorate even without underlying segment changes. Annual payment dominates over instalment options. Diesel vehicles outnumber gasoline by roughly two to one. Urban and rural circulation are close to balanced (54% vs 46%), though within-category loss-ratio profiles differ markedly as Section 4.5 shows. Interior locations dominate the geographic distribution (65%), with coastal and islands together accounting for 35%; despite their smaller volume, the islands segment carries the widest within-category loss-ratio spread.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3.4 Distribution of derived KPIs
The three derived KPIs are themselves variables worth profiling. At the policy level, they are highly skewed: most policies have no claims, so most loss ratios and frequencies are zero. Restricting the view to policies with at least one claim reveals the within-distribution shape that matters for segment-level analysis.


Show the code
share_above_be <- clean |>
  filter(total_claims > 0, is.finite(loss_ratio)) |>
  summarise(share = mean(loss_ratio > 1)) |>
  pull(share)

clean |>
  filter(total_claims > 0, is.finite(loss_ratio),
         loss_ratio >= 0.01, loss_ratio <= 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio, fill = loss_ratio > 1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, boundary = 1, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    trans  = "log10",
    breaks = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100),
    labels = c("1%", "10%", "100%", "1,000%", "10,000%")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = house_muted, "TRUE" = house_highlight),
    guide  = "none"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = house_benchmark) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.15, y = Inf,
    label  = "Break-even (100%)",
    hjust  = 0, vjust = 1.2,
    colour = house_benchmark, size = 3.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "A substantial share of claim-bearing policies exceed break-even",
    subtitle = paste0(
      scales::percent(share_above_be, accuracy = 0.1),
      " of claim-bearing policy-years have losses exceeding their premium"
    ),
    x       = "Loss ratio (log scale)",
    y       = "Policy-years",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data)."
  ) +
  theme_house()









Among policies with at least one claim, the loss-ratio distribution spans nearly four orders of magnitude. The dashed grey line marks the break-even point where losses equal premium. The red bars to the right represent policy-years that returned more in claims than they collected in premium. Segment-level mean loss ratios mask this within-policy variance, which is what the volatility (coefficient of variation) analysis in Section 4 surfaces.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3.5 Summary of univariate observations
The univariate view raises three structural features the bivariate analysis must contend with:

Strong distributional skew in vehicle value and the derived KPIs. Linear-scale plots will mislead. Log scales and percentile bands are appropriate.
Heavy class imbalance in bonus_score (concentrated in Good) and policy_type (concentrated in CC and COMP_E). Statistical tests must account for unequal group sizes.
The zero-claim majority. Roughly 85% of policy-years have no claims, making policy-level loss ratio a noisy individual measure but a clean segment-level one when aggregated by exposure-weighted sums.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3.6 Pairwise relationships among continuous variables
Before turning to bivariate analysis of the categorical risk drivers, the continuous variables are examined jointly through a correlation matrix. The correlogram surfaces three things: which variable pairs move together strongly enough to constrain interpretation downstream, which appear independent and can be treated as separate signals, and whether any pair carries multicollinearity that would distort multivariate inference.


Show the code
cont_vars <- clean |>
  select(driver_age, vehicle_age, age_driving_licence,
         vehicle_value, seats, power_to_weight_ratio,
         total_premium, total_exposure, loss_ratio) |>
  filter(if_all(everything(), is.finite))

corr_matrix <- cor(cont_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs",
                   method = "spearman")

p_matrix <- cor_pmat(cont_vars, method = "spearman")

ggcorrplot(corr_matrix,
           type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE,
           lab_size = 3,
           p.mat = p_matrix,
           sig.level = 0.05,
           insig = "blank",
           colors = c("#4C72B0", "white", house_highlight),
           outline.color = "white",
           tl.cex = 9) +
  labs(
    title = "Driver age and licence tenure are the strongest pair",
    subtitle = "Spearman correlations among continuous variables; non-significant cells (p ≥ 0.05) blanked",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    fill = "Spearman ρ",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nSpearman rank correlation used because several variables are heavily skewed."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "right",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 15, b = 30, l = 30))









Three patterns are visible. The strongest correlation in the matrix is between driver_age and age_driving_licence (ρ = 0.86), which is structural and expected: older drivers have held licences longer. A second strong association sits between total_premium and total_exposure (ρ = 0.74), also structural, since premium earned scales with the on-risk period of a policy. The most analytically interesting cell is the moderate negative correlation between vehicle_value and power_to_weight_ratio (ρ = -0.5), indicating that higher-value vehicles in this portfolio tend to be heavier sedans rather than performance vehicles, the opposite of the pattern in younger, sportier markets. Beyond these three, all remaining pairs are weak. loss_ratio in particular shows only weak correlations with the underlying predictors, confirming that no single continuous variable explains policy-level loss outcomes on its own. This is the empirical motivation for the segment-level bivariate analysis that follows: where individual continuous variables fail to discriminate, categorical and joint structure may succeed.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4.1 Methodology
The bivariate analysis investigates how the portfolio’s policy, vehicle, driver, and geographic characteristics relate to its profitability (loss ratio) and volatility (coefficient of variation of loss ratio across policies within a segment).
Four analytical principles guide the work:

Segment-level loss ratio, not policy-level. Individual policies have highly skewed loss ratios, since most are zero and a few are very large. Aggregating to the segment level via sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium) produces the exposure-weighted metric an underwriter would price against.
Statistical validation alongside every visual claim. Where the relationship is categorical, ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats or ggbarstats provides inline test annotations (ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square). Where the comparison is across years on a ratio of sums, bootstrap confidence intervals are used because the sampling distribution of a ratio is not well-described by closed-form parametric tests.
Volatility reported alongside profitability. A segment with high mean loss ratio is unprofitable. A segment with high CV of loss ratio is unpredictable. Underwriting interventions for these two cases differ and should not be conflated.
Multiple-comparison correction is applied within tests, not across the report. The pairwise comparisons within each ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats and ggbarstats call use false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. No correction is applied across the report-wide family of tests. Given the sample size (>350,000 records) and the magnitude of the effects discussed, the substantive findings are robust to multiple-comparison concerns, but readers interpreting individual p-values should bear the report-wide test count in mind.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4.2 Temporal trajectory
The first question to ask of any insurance portfolio is whether the recent loss experience is stable, improving, or worsening. The aggregate view by year shows clear movement.

    n_pol    = n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    frequency  = claims / exposure,
    severity   = incurred / claims
  )

yr |>
  select(year, n_pol, premium, incurred, loss_ratio, frequency, severity) |>
  kable(

Three movements show up at once. Loss ratio rose from approximately 66% in 2022 to 75% in 2024, a 9-percentage-point swing in two years. Frequency edged up modestly. Severity increased more meaningfully, indicating that average claim cost rather than claim count is the principal driver. To establish whether this trajectory is real or a small-sample artefact, the bootstrap distribution of loss ratio is computed for each year.


Show the code
set.seed(608)
B <- 500

boot_one_year <- function(df, B) {
  n <- nrow(df)
  prem <- df$total_premium
  inc  <- df$total_incurred
  replicate(B, {
    idx <- sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE)
    sum(inc[idx]) / sum(prem[idx])
  })
}

boot_df <- clean |>
  filter(total_premium > 0) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  group_modify(~ tibble(loss_ratio = boot_one_year(.x, B))) |>
  ungroup()


boot_summary <- boot_df |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    lr_median = median(loss_ratio),
    lr_lower = quantile(loss_ratio, 0.025),
    lr_upper = quantile(loss_ratio, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = loss_ratio, y = factor(year))) +
  stat_halfeye(aes(fill = factor(year)),
               .width = c(.95), point_interval = "mean_qi",
               alpha = 0.8, slab_colour = "white", slab_linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.70, linetype = "dashed", colour = house_benchmark) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.70, y = 3.55, label = "70% benchmark",
           hjust = 1.05, size = 3, colour = "grey40", fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("curve",
           x = 0.78, xend = 0.745,
           y = 3.2, yend = 3.1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = 0.3, colour = house_highlight, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 0.79, y = 3.25,
           label = "2024 distribution sits\nentirely above earlier years",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = house_highlight, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0.6, 0.85)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("2022" = "grey75",
                                "2023" = "grey55",
                                "2024" = house_highlight),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "2024 loss ratio is well outside the prior-year range",
    subtitle = "Bootstrap distribution of portfolio loss ratio by year (500 resamples)",
    x = "Bootstrap loss ratio",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data)."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11)









The 95% intervals for 2022 and 2023 overlap substantially, but the 2024 distribution sits entirely above both prior years. The intervals are well-separated and statistically distinct. The deterioration is a real shift, not sampling noise.


Show the code
yr_per_pol <- yr |>
  mutate(
    premium_per_pol = premium / n_pol,
    incurred_per_pol = incurred / n_pol
  ) |>
  select(year, premium_per_pol, incurred_per_pol) |>
  pivot_longer(c(premium_per_pol, incurred_per_pol),
               names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric,
                          levels = c("premium_per_pol", "incurred_per_pol"),
                          labels = c("Premium per policy (€)",
                                     "Incurred losses per policy (€)")))

ggplot(yr_per_pol, aes(x = year, y = value, colour = metric, group = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("€", round(value))),
            vjust = -1.4, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2022, 2023, 2024)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.1, 0.25))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Premium per policy (€)" = house_benchmark,
                                  "Incurred losses per policy (€)" = house_highlight)) +
  labs(
    title = "Incurred losses rose faster than premium across the period",
    subtitle = "Per-policy economics, 2022–2024",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Euros per policy",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nThe deterioration is decomposed in the following table."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









The aggregate decomposition shows a clear gap: premium per policy rose from €278 in 2022 to €303 in 2024 (a 9 percent increase), while incurred losses per policy rose from €183 to €226 (a 24 percent increase). Average frequency and average severity remained nearly flat across the period (frequency 0.302 to 0.311, severity €969 to €971). The portfolio-level deterioration therefore did not arise from a uniform rise in claim incidence or claim size. Where the deterioration originates is not yet clear from the aggregate view. A decomposition follows.
A standard within-versus-between decomposition isolates the source of the 8.9-percentage-point loss-ratio swing. The 2022 portfolio loss ratio is recomputed three ways: (i) with 2022 segment loss ratios and 2022 segment weights (the actual 2022 value), (ii) with 2024 segment loss ratios but 2022 segment weights (the within-segment effect: how much the deterioration would have been if mix had stayed constant), and (iii) with 2022 segment loss ratios but 2024 segment weights (the between-segment effect: how much the deterioration would have been if segments themselves hadn’t moved). The residual is the interaction. Segments are defined by policy type, the dimension that dominated the bivariate findings.


Show the code
seg_year <- clean |>
  filter(total_premium > 0) |>
  group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    premium = sum(total_premium),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred),
    lr = incurred / premium,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(weight = premium / sum(premium)) |>
  ungroup()

lr_2022 <- seg_year |> filter(year == 2022) |> select(policy_type, lr_2022 = lr, w_2022 = weight)
lr_2024 <- seg_year |> filter(year == 2024) |> select(policy_type, lr_2024 = lr, w_2024 = weight)

decomp <- lr_2022 |>
  full_join(lr_2024, by = "policy_type") |>
  mutate(
    contrib_within  = w_2022 * (lr_2024 - lr_2022),
    contrib_between = lr_2022 * (w_2024 - w_2022),
    contrib_interaction = (lr_2024 - lr_2022) * (w_2024 - w_2022)
  )

decomp_summary <- tibble(
  component = c("Actual 2022 → 2024 swing",
                "Within-segment effect (segments worsened)",
                "Between-segment effect (mix shifted)",
                "Interaction"),
  value = c(
    sum(decomp$lr_2024 * decomp$w_2024) - sum(decomp$lr_2022 * decomp$w_2022),
    sum(decomp$contrib_within),
    sum(decomp$contrib_between),
    sum(decomp$contrib_interaction)
  )
)

decomp_summary |>
  mutate(value = scales::percent(value, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Decomposition of 2022 → 2024 portfolio loss-ratio swing")



Decomposition of 2022 → 2024 portfolio loss-ratio swing


component
value




Actual 2022 → 2024 swing

Within-segment effect (segments worsened)

The decomposition is unambiguous. The within-segment effect accounts for 8.5 of the 8.9-percentage-point swing, while the between-segment effect contributes only 0.1pp and the interaction 0.4pp. The portfolio’s deterioration is therefore driven by segments themselves becoming less profitable over the period, not by a shift in business volume toward worse-performing segments. The book’s policy-type composition was stable; what changed was the loss ratio within each existing segment. The bivariate analysis in the remainder of Section 4 identifies which specific segments deteriorated and where premium adequacy is most strained, beginning with the policy-type gradient in Section 4.3.

Show the code
clean |>

                     labels = c("1%", "10%", "100%", "1,000%", "10,000%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TP"     = "grey75",
                                "TPG"    = "grey75",
                                "CC"     = "grey75",
                                "COMP_E" = "grey75",
                                "COMP_N" = house_highlight),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "COMP_N's loss-ratio distribution sits visibly to the right of every other tier",
    subtitle = "Ridgeline densities of policy-level loss ratio across five coverage tiers (claims-positive policies, log scale)",
    x = "Loss ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nWhite vertical lines mark the within-tier median."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 25, r = 15, b = 15, l = 10))











Show the code
clean |>
  filter(total_claims > 0,
         is.finite(loss_ratio),
         loss_ratio >= 0.05, loss_ratio <= 50) |>
  ggbetweenstats(
    x = policy_type,
    y = loss_ratio,
    type = "np",
    pairwise.display = "significant",
    p.adjust.method = "fdr",
    plot.type = "boxviolin",
    centrality.plotting = TRUE,
    bf.message = FALSE,
    ggtheme = theme_minimal()
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TP" = "grey60",
                                  "TPG" = "grey60",
                                  "CC" = "grey60",
                                  "COMP_E" = "grey60",
                                  "COMP_N" = house_highlight),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TP" = "grey60",
                                "TPG" = "grey60",
                                "CC" = "grey60",
                                "COMP_E" = "grey60",
                                "COMP_N" = house_highlight),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans  = "log10",
    breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 20),
    labels = c("10%", "50%", "100%", "500%", "2,000%")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.05, 50)) +
  labs(x = "Policy type",
       y = "Policy-level loss ratio (log scale, claims-positive only)")









The Kruskal-Wallis test on policy-level loss ratio rejects the null of equal distributions across policy types at any conventional significance level. Pairwise comparisons (FDR-adjusted) confirm that COMP_N is significantly different from every other tier. The finding represents a systematic pricing inadequacy rather than statistical noise.
The diagnosis is that comprehensive-without-excess is sold at premium levels that do not reflect its actual loss exposure. Swiss Re’s framework describes this pattern as a premium and exposure mismatch.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4.4 The bonus-malus paradox
bonus_score is the insurer’s primary mechanism for adjusting premium to historical claim behaviour. Three categories are used: Good (no recent claims), Neutral (intermediate), and Bad (recent claims history). The expectation is straightforward. Claim frequency should rise from Good to Bad, and loss ratio should follow, unless the pricing applied to Bad policies has already absorbed their elevated frequency.

bs |>

    caption = "Portfolio KPIs by bonus-malus category",

The frequency column behaves as expected: 0.30 for Good, 0.48 for Neutral, 0.62 for Bad, a clean monotonic rise. Premium per exposure also rises monotonically, as the bonus-malus surcharges intend. The loss ratio tells a different story.


Show the code
bs_se <- clean |>
  group_by(bonus_score) |>
  summarise(
    n_pol      = n(),
    incurred   = sum(total_incurred),
    premium    = sum(total_premium),
    exposure   = sum(total_exposure),
    claims     = sum(total_claims),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    lr_se      = sqrt((incurred / premium) * (1 - incurred / premium) / premium),
    lr_lower   = pmax(0, loss_ratio - 1.96 * lr_se),
    lr_upper   = loss_ratio + 1.96 * lr_se,
    frequency  = claims / exposure,
    freq_se    = sqrt(claims) / exposure,
    freq_lower = pmax(0, frequency - 1.96 * freq_se),
    freq_upper = frequency + 1.96 * freq_se,
    avg_prem   = premium / exposure,
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(highlight = if_else(bonus_score == "Neutral", "Neutral", "Other"))

panel_style <- list(
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Neutral" = house_highlight,
                                  "Other" = house_benchmark),
                      guide = "none"),
  theme_house(base_size = 10),
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey20",
                                     size = 10, margin = margin(b = 5)))
)

p_lr <- ggplot(bs_se, aes(x = bonus_score, y = loss_ratio, colour = highlight)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lr_lower, ymax = lr_upper), width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)),
            vjust = -1.6, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.45))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Loss ratio", subtitle = "Loss ratio (with 95% CI)") +
  panel_style

p_freq <- ggplot(bs_se, aes(x = bonus_score, y = frequency, colour = highlight)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = freq_lower, ymax = freq_upper), width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(frequency, 3)),
            vjust = -1.6, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.45))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Frequency", subtitle = "Claim frequency (claims per policy-year)") +
  panel_style

p_prem <- ggplot(bs_se, aes(x = bonus_score, y = avg_prem, colour = highlight)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("€", round(avg_prem))),
            vjust = -1.6, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.45))) +
  labs(x = "Bonus-malus category", y = "Premium / exposure (€)",
       subtitle = "Average premium per unit of exposure") +
  panel_style

(p_lr / p_freq / p_prem) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Neutral pays less but loses more: the bonus-malus paradox",
    subtitle = "Loss ratio, frequency, and premium per exposure by bonus-malus category, 2022–2024",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data). \n95% confidence intervals from binomial (loss ratio) and Poisson (frequency) approximations.",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10, margin = margin(b = 12)),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey50", size = 8, hjust = 0)
    )
  )









The three-panel composite makes the paradox visible. Frequency rises monotonically across Good, Neutral, and Bad (0.30, 0.48, 0.62 claims per policy-year), and average premium per exposure does the same (€408, €668, €899). Loss ratio does not follow that pattern. Neutral runs at 81.9 percent, materially above the 79.6 percent of Bad, despite collecting 26 percent less premium per exposure. The 95% confidence intervals on loss ratio and frequency confirm that the gap is not noise. The bonus-malus mechanism is absorbing the elevated frequency in the Bad tier but not in Neutral.


Show the code
clean |>
  filter(total_claims > 0,
         is.finite(loss_ratio),
         loss_ratio >= 0.05, loss_ratio <= 50) |>
  ggbetweenstats(
    x = bonus_score,
    y = loss_ratio,
    type = "np",
    pairwise.display = "significant",
    p.adjust.method = "fdr",
    plot.type = "boxviolin",
    bf.message = FALSE,
    ggtheme = theme_minimal()
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Good" = "grey60",
                                  "Neutral" = house_highlight,
                                  "Bad" = "grey60"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Good" = "grey60",
                                "Neutral" = house_highlight,
                                "Bad" = "grey60"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans  = "log10",
    breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 20),
    labels = c("10%", "50%", "100%", "500%", "2,000%")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.05, 50)) +
  labs(x = "Bonus-malus category",
       y = "Policy-level loss ratio (log scale, claims-positive only)")









The chart shows policy-level loss ratio among claims-positive policies, which inverts the directional pattern of the segment-level aggregate above. Good-tier policies have the lowest premium, so a single claim produces a high policy-level ratio; the segment-level view is dominated instead by the much larger share of zero-claim policies. The statistical test confirms that the Neutral and Bad distributions differ, and that Good is materially separated from both. The Neutral segment is the pricing gap. Two non-exclusive explanations are plausible:

New entrants land in Neutral by default, before sufficient claim history has accumulated to move them up or down, and the default premium does not load adequately for the embedded risk in this group.
Bonus-malus transitions are downward-rigid: a policyholder who claims may stay in Neutral rather than move to Bad, again undercharging for actual loss potential.

Section 5 (panel transition analysis) examines the second hypothesis directly by tracking individual policyholders across years.

4.6 Driver age and vehicle age: a risk surface
Driver age and vehicle age are continuous variables. Examining them jointly via the loss-ratio surface reveals which combinations carry the highest expected losses, beyond what either variable alone would suggest.

age_interaction <- clean |>

The 25 to 49 driver bands show flatter loss-ratio profiles across vehicle ages, indicating that the interaction effect is concentrated in the youngest driver segment. The 65+ band shows a mild upward drift in newer vehicles, consistent with senior drivers in higher-value vehicles carrying distinct loss profiles.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4.7 Volatility view
Profitability and volatility are conceptually distinct. A segment can have a low mean loss ratio with high variance, making it unpredictable even if it averages out acceptably. The coefficient of variation of policy-level loss ratio captures this directly.
Policies with non-finite loss ratios (caused by zero or missing premium values) are removed before computing volatility, to avoid distortion from undefined ratios.


Show the code
rvol <- clean |>
  filter(total_claims > 0,
         is.finite(loss_ratio),
         !is.na(loss_ratio)) |>
  group_by(policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    n_pol = n(),
    sd_lr = sd(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

vol <- pt |>
  select(policy_type, n_pol, loss_ratio) |>
  rename(segment_lr = loss_ratio) |>
  left_join(rvol |> select(policy_type, sd_lr), by = "policy_type") |>
  mutate(cv_lr = sd_lr / segment_lr)

vol |>
  kable(
    caption = "Segment-level loss ratio and within-segment volatility",
    digits = c(0, 0, 4, 3, 3),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  )



Segment-level loss ratio and within-segment volatility

The coefficient of variation here is defined as the policy-level standard deviation of loss ratio (among claims-positive policies) divided by the segment-level loss ratio. The numerator captures the within-segment dispersion an underwriter would face when pricing an individual policy in that segment; the denominator captures the segment’s exposure-weighted central tendency. The two are computed at different levels of aggregation by design. A purely policy-level CV would weight each policy equally regardless of premium, while a purely segment-level CV (e.g., via bootstrap) would describe the segment-mean estimator’s uncertainty rather than the within-segment dispersion across policies. The chosen definition prioritises the underwriter’s perspective on individual-policy variance.


Show the code
vol <- vol |>
  mutate(highlight = if_else(policy_type == "COMP_N", "COMP_N", "Other"))

ggplot(vol, aes(x = segment_lr, y = cv_lr)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(vol$cv_lr),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = house_benchmark) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.70,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = house_benchmark) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_pol, colour = highlight), alpha = 0.85) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = policy_type, colour = highlight),
                           size = 3.8, fontface = "bold",
                           point.padding = 0.8, box.padding = 0.6,
                           min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1,
                           show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.71, y = 5,
           label = "70% benchmark", hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = house_benchmark, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.52, y = mean(vol$cv_lr) + 4,
           label = "Portfolio mean CV", hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = house_benchmark, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0.5, 1.0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 140),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_size(range = c(4, 14), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("COMP_N" = house_highlight,
                                  "Other" = house_benchmark),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "COMP_N is the worst-performing tier but the most predictable",
    subtitle = "Segment loss ratio versus within-segment volatility, bubble area proportional to policy count",
    x = "Segment loss ratio (profitability axis)",
    y = "Coefficient of variation (volatility axis)",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nBubble size: number of policies in segment. Reference lines: 70% loss-ratio benchmark and portfolio-mean CV."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11)









The two-axis view separates profitability from predictability. COMP_N has the worst segment loss ratio at 93.5% but the lowest within-segment volatility (CV 7.6), meaning its loss experience is unprofitable but highly predictable. COMP_E shows the opposite profile: a moderately high mean loss ratio of 73.9% paired with the highest volatility in the portfolio (CV 123), driven by occasional large-severity claims that dominate the segment’s variance. CC combines a moderate segment loss ratio of 63.5% with mid-range volatility, the most balanced profile in the book.
These two segments illustrate that profitability and predictability operate on independent dimensions. COMP_N is unprofitable but predictable, while COMP_E is closer to break-even on average and its tail risk dominates the within-segment variance.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4.8 Section summary
The bivariate analysis identifies four loss drivers:

Temporal deterioration. The 2022 to 2024 loss-ratio trajectory shows a statistically validated worsening, with severity contributing more than frequency.
Coverage tier mispricing. COMP_N runs a loss ratio of 93.5%, materially worse than every other tier and statistically distinct in pairwise testing.
Bonus-malus paradox. The Neutral category carries the highest loss ratio in the portfolio despite middle-of-the-road claim frequency, suggesting either default-tier under-loading or downward-rigid bonus-malus transitions. Section 5 examines the transition dynamics directly.
Geographic and age-driven concentration. Urban island policies and young-driver-old-vehicle combinations both show elevated loss intensity, with the latter representing a joint pattern that additive treatment of the two age dimensions would miss.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
5.1 Bonus-malus transitions over time
The same policyholder can appear in 2022, 2023, and 2024 records. This creates a panel structure that single-year cross-sectional analysis discards. The bonus-malus paradox identified in Section 4 (Neutral carrying higher loss ratio than Bad) raised the question of whether bonus-score transitions are downward-rigid. A Sankey diagram of category transitions answers this directly.


Show the code
trans_22_24 <- clean |>
  select(insured_id, year, bonus_score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = bonus_score,
              names_prefix = "y") |>
  filter(!is.na(y2022), !is.na(y2024)) |>
  filter(!(y2022 == "Good" & y2024 == "Good")) |>
  count(y2022, y2024, name = "policies") |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("y"), ~ factor(.x, levels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad"))))

ggplot(trans_22_24,
       aes(axis1 = y2022, axis2 = y2024, y = policies)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = y2022), alpha = 0.75, width = 0.3,
                colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_stratum(width = 0.3, fill = "grey90", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)),
            size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("2022", "2024"), expand = c(0.1, 0.1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Good" = "#4C72B0",
                                "Neutral" = "#DDB237",
                                "Bad" = "#C44E52"),
                    name = "2022 starting category") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Recovery dominates: most non-Good policyholders improved by 2024",
    subtitle = "Bonus-malus transitions 2022 to 2024 (stable-Good policyholders excluded)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Policyholders",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\nPolicyholders observed in both 2022 and 2024; stable-Good excluded."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









The Sankey reveals the structure of bonus-malus dynamics among policyholders whose category changed at least once between 2022 and 2024. (Policyholders who remained Good throughout, the largest single group at around 99 percent of the panel, are excluded to surface the transition dynamics.) Among the remaining policyholders, upward movement dominates: most who started in Neutral improved to Good, and most who started in Bad improved to Neutral or Good. A smaller but visible flow shows Good policyholders who moved downward into Neutral or Bad. The mechanism therefore favours recovery rather than long-term entrapment, but it also does not protect Good policyholders from downward drift entirely.


Show the code
trans_summary <- clean |>

  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = bonus_score,
              names_prefix = "y") |>
  filter(!is.na(y2022), !is.na(y2024)) |>
  mutate(
    move = case_when(
      y2022 == y2024 ~ "Stayed",
      as.integer(y2022) < as.integer(y2024) ~ "Worsened",
      TRUE ~ "Improved"
    )
  ) |>

  group_by(y2022) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

trans_summary |>

The transition table clarifies the pattern. Good policyholders are highly persistent, with 99.6% remaining Good between 2022 and 2024. Neutral and Bad policyholders mostly improve over the same period: 86.0% of Neutral policyholders improve, while 78.8% of Bad policyholders improve. The bonus-malus mechanism therefore appears to allow recovery from worse categories, rather than trapping policyholders there. The pricing concern surfaced in Section 4.4 is the short-term loss-ratio behaviour of policyholders while they sit in the Neutral and Bad pools, rather than any structural transition rigidity.
This result partially adjudicates the two hypotheses raised in Section 4.4. The downward-rigid transitions hypothesis is not supported by the data: policyholders in worse categories overwhelmingly improve rather than remain stuck. The default-tier under-loading hypothesis remains plausible and is consistent with the elevated short-term loss ratio observed in the Neutral pool, though confirming it would require examining the entry composition of the Neutral category over time, which sits beyond the scope of the present exercise. Future research applying a formal longitudinal model of bonus-malus dynamics could discriminate between these explanations more rigorously.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
5.2 Lorenz curve of loss concentration
A second question worth asking of the portfolio is how unevenly losses are distributed across the population of policies. In a perfectly homogeneous book, every policy would contribute the same share of losses. In a heterogeneous book, a small fraction of policies accounts for the bulk of incurred losses, which is what underwriters mean when they refer to a “concentration of losses.” The Lorenz curve visualises this.


Show the code
lor <- clean |>
  arrange(total_incurred) |>
  mutate(
    cum_policies = row_number() / n(),
    cum_incurred = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred)
  )

gini_value <- 1 - 2 * sum((lor$cum_incurred + lag(lor$cum_incurred, default = 0)) / 2) / nrow(lor)
gini_value <- round(gini_value, 3)




Show the code
lor <- clean |>
  arrange(total_incurred) |>
  mutate(
    cum_pol = row_number() / n(),
    cum_incurred = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred)
  )

gini_value <- 1 - 2 * sum((lor$cum_pol[-1] - lor$cum_pol[-nrow(lor)]) *
                            (lor$cum_incurred[-1] + lor$cum_incurred[-nrow(lor)]) / 2)

p90_loss_share <- 1 - lor$cum_incurred[which.min(abs(lor$cum_pol - 0.9))]

ggplot(lor, aes(x = cum_pol, y = cum_incurred)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", colour = house_benchmark) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = cum_incurred, ymax = cum_pol),
              fill = house_highlight, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = house_highlight, linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 0.55, y = 0.62,
           label = "Equity line\n(perfect equality)",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "grey45",
           fontface = "italic", lineheight = 0.95) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 0.35, y = 0.05,
           label = paste0("Gini = ", round(gini_value, 3)),
           hjust = 0, size = 5, colour = house_highlight,
           fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("curve",
           x = 0.78, xend = 0.93,
           y = 0.18, yend = 0.28,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = -0.3, colour = house_highlight, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 0.77, y = 0.14,
           label = paste0("Top 10% of policyholders\nbear ",
                          round(p90_loss_share * 100),
                          "% of incurred losses"),
           hjust = 1, size = 3.1, colour = house_highlight, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Top 10% of policyholders bear ",
                   round(p90_loss_share * 100),
                   "% of incurred losses"),
    subtitle = paste0("Lorenz curve of cumulative incurred losses (Gini = ",
                      round(gini_value, 3), ")"),
    x = "Cumulative share of policyholders (sorted by incurred)",
    y = "Cumulative share of incurred losses",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data)."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11)









The interpretation is direct. The dashed diagonal represents perfect equality, where the bottom X% of policies would account for X% of losses. The red curve shows reality. The bottom 85% of policies (those with no claims) contribute zero losses. The top 5% of policies account for the majority of total incurred. The Gini coefficient is approximately 0.956, indicating extreme concentration.


Show the code
decile_view <- clean |>
  arrange(total_incurred) |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(total_incurred, 10)) |>
  group_by(decile) |>
  summarise(
    n_pol = n(),
    share_premium = sum(total_premium) / sum(clean$total_premium),
    share_incurred = sum(total_incurred) / sum(clean$total_incurred),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

decile_long <- decile_view |>
  pivot_longer(c(share_premium, share_incurred),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric,
                          levels = c("share_premium", "share_incurred"),
                          labels = c("Share of premium",
                                     "Share of incurred")))

top10_premium <- decile_view$share_premium[10]
top10_incurred <- decile_view$share_incurred[10]

ggplot(decile_long, aes(x = factor(decile), y = share, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(data = decile_long |> filter(decile == 10),
            aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold",
            colour = c(house_benchmark, house_highlight)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Share of premium"  = house_benchmark,
                                "Share of incurred" = house_highlight),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("The top decile contributes ",
                   percent(top10_premium, accuracy = 1),
                   " of premium but ",
                   percent(top10_incurred, accuracy = 1),
                   " of incurred losses"),
    subtitle = "Premium and incurred-loss shares by decile of policies (ranked low to high by incurred losses)",
    x = "Decile of policies",
    y = "Share of portfolio total",
    caption = "Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data)."
  ) +
  theme_house(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









The decile view sharpens the Lorenz finding. The top decile of policies accounts for the overwhelming share of incurred losses. The premium share contributed by the same decile is significantly smaller. The two-axis gap shows that premium charged does not currently scale with incurred losses, which is the empirical manifestation of the segment-level mismatches diagnosed in Section 4.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
section: 5.3 Cluster heatmap of segment risk profiles
text:
5.3 Cluster heatmap of segment risk profiles
Segments examined one variable at a time can mask the multivariate structure of risk. Two segments may share a moderate loss ratio while behaving very differently on frequency, severity, and premium adequacy. A cluster heatmap addresses this by computing a multi-metric profile for each segment, standardising the metrics to a common scale, and using hierarchical clustering to group segments that share similar profiles. The dendrogram makes the clustering visible. The dendrogram is cut at k = 3 because a two-cluster cut would collapse the analytically distinct singleton into the main book, while a four-cluster cut would over-fragment the largest group without surfacing additional structure; k = 3 is the smallest cut that exposes both the high-loss singleton and the elevated-COMP_N pair.


Show the code
seg_profile <- clean |>
  filter(total_premium > 0, total_exposure > 0) |>
  group_by(policy_type, bonus_score) |>
  summarise(
    n_pol      = n(),
    loss_ratio = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
    frequency  = sum(total_claims) / sum(total_exposure),
    severity   = if_else(sum(total_claims) > 0,
                         sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_claims),
                         NA_real_),
    avg_prem   = sum(total_premium) / sum(total_exposure),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_pol >= 100, !is.na(severity)) |>
  mutate(segment = paste(policy_type, bonus_score, sep = " · ")) |>
  select(segment, loss_ratio, frequency, severity, avg_prem)

seg_matrix <- seg_profile |>
  column_to_rownames("segment") |>
  scale() |>
  as.matrix()




Show the code
row_hclust <- hclust(dist(seg_matrix),     method = "complete")
col_hclust <- hclust(dist(t(seg_matrix)),  method = "complete")

k_row        <- 3
row_clusters <- cutree(row_hclust, k = k_row)
N            <- length(row_hclust$order)
M            <- length(col_hclust$order)

cut_height <- mean(row_hclust$height[c(N - k_row, N - k_row + 1)])

row_order <- row_hclust$labels[row_hclust$order]
col_order <- col_hclust$labels[col_hclust$order]

classify_segment <- function(x, xend, y, yend) {
  if (max(y, yend) >= cut_height) return(NA_character_)
  mid_pos <- round((x + xend) / 2)
  mid_pos <- max(1, min(N, mid_pos))
  label   <- row_hclust$labels[row_hclust$order[mid_pos]]
  as.character(row_clusters[label])
}

row_ddata <- dendro_data(as.dendrogram(row_hclust), type = "rectangle")
row_segs  <- segment(row_ddata) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(cluster = classify_segment(x, xend, y, yend)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster, levels = as.character(seq_len(k_row))))

col_ddata <- dendro_data(as.dendrogram(col_hclust), type = "rectangle")
col_segs  <- segment(col_ddata)

heat_long <- seg_matrix |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("segment") |>
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "metric", values_to = "z") |>
  mutate(
    segment = factor(segment, levels = row_order),
    metric  = factor(metric,  levels = col_order)
  )

cluster_palette <- c("1" = house_highlight,
                     "2" = "#4C72B0",
                     "3" = "grey50")

p_row <- ggplot(row_segs) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = y, y = x, xend = yend, yend = xend,
                   colour = cluster),
               linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_reverse(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, N + 0.5),
                     expand = c(0, 0),
                     breaks = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values   = cluster_palette,
                      na.value = "grey60",
                      guide    = "none") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 30, l = 5))

p_col <- ggplot(col_segs) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, M + 0.5),
                     expand = c(0, 0),
                     breaks = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0)),
                     breaks = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 5, b = 0, l = 0))

p_heat <- ggplot(heat_long, aes(x = metric, y = segment, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", z)),
            size = 2.8, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low      = "#4C72B0",
                       mid      = "white",
                       high     = house_highlight,
                       midpoint = 0,
                       name     = "Z-score") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0), position = "bottom") +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid        = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x       = element_text(size = 9),
        axis.text.y       = element_text(size = 8.5),
        legend.position   = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(1.2, "cm"),
        plot.margin       = margin(t = 5, r = 5, b = 5, l = 0))

(patchwork::plot_spacer() + p_col +
   p_row + p_heat) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, widths = c(1, 4), heights = c(1, 4)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Segments cluster into three distinct risk profiles",
    subtitle = paste0("Hierarchical clustering of segments and metrics ",
                      "(Euclidean distance, complete linkage); ",
                      "rows coloured by k = 3 cut"),
    caption  = paste0("Source: Spanish motor insurance portfolio (Mendeley Data).\n",
                      "Metrics scaled to z-scores prior to clustering. ",
                      "Branch colours indicate the three row clusters; ",
                      "shared trunk segments shown in grey."),
    theme = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 10,
                                   margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption  = element_text(colour = "grey50", size = 8, hjust = 0)
    )
  )









The clustering algorithm groups segments by similarity across all four standardised metrics simultaneously. Three groups emerge. The largest spans eleven segments, covering TP, TPG, CC, and COMP_E across all bonus tiers, together with COMP_N · Good, all sharing balanced profiles close to the portfolio mean. The second cluster is a tight pair, COMP_N · Neutral and COMP_N · Bad, defined by elevated frequency and average premium. The third is a singleton, TPG · Bad, isolated by its very high loss ratio and severity. The result sharpens the COMP_N diagnosis from Section 4.3. The elevated loss intensity is not uniform across the COMP_N product; it sits in the two bonus-malus tiers (Neutral and Bad) where Section 4.4 already identified premium inadequacy. The clustering and the bonus-malus paradox therefore point to the same pattern from two angles. The dendrogram quantifies the separations: the largest vertical jump isolates TPG · Bad, with the COMP_N · Neutral and COMP_N · Bad pair separating from the main group at the next level down.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
6.1 Key findings

The portfolio loss ratio rose from 65.7 percent in 2022 to 74.7 percent in 2024. The deterioration is statistically validated through non-overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals, and a within-versus-between decomposition shows that 8.5 of the 8.9-percentage-point swing arises from within-segment deterioration rather than from a mix shift toward worse-performing segments. Claim severity rather than claim frequency dominates the aggregate trend.
Loss ratio varies monotonically across coverage tiers, from 54 percent in basic third-party to approximately 94 percent in comprehensive-without-excess (COMP_N). Pairwise non-parametric tests confirm that COMP_N is statistically distinct from every other tier.
The bonus-malus categories show an unexpected pattern: the Neutral tier carries a higher loss ratio than the Bad tier despite collecting less premium per exposure. Frequency rises monotonically across the three categories as expected, but the loss-ratio ordering inverts at the top.
Geographic loss intensity differs sharply within municipality categories. Urban island policies run 11 percentage points above rural island policies, the widest within-category spread in the geographic dimension.
Driver age and vehicle age interact non-additively in their relationship with loss ratio. The under-25 driver band paired with older vehicles shows the highest loss intensity in the joint surface.
Coverage tier and bonus-malus interact in the multivariate clustering. The elevated loss profile is not uniform across COMP_N: it concentrates in the Neutral and Bad bonus tiers, which cluster as a tight pair, while COMP_N · Good sits with the main book. The clustering corroborates the bonus-malus paradox identified in Section 4.4 from a different methodological angle.
Loss concentration is extreme. The Lorenz curve of incurred losses yields a Gini coefficient of approximately 0.96, with the top decile of policies bearing approximately 99 percent of total incurred losses.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
6.2 Recommendations for future research

Confirmatory analysis. This study is exploratory. Future work should apply formal causal-inference methods to confirm whether the segment-level loss-ratio differences reflect underlying risk heterogeneity or unobserved confounding.
Additional variables. The Mendeley dataset is rich on policy and vehicle characteristics but contains no driving-behaviour telematics, no claim-type detail beyond seven coverage categories, and no geographic granularity below the municipality type. Incorporating these would refine the segment-level diagnostics.
Longitudinal modelling. The panel structure used in the Sankey analysis could be extended to a full longitudinal model of policyholder transitions, including survival analysis of policy cancellation and Markov chain modelling of bonus-malus dynamics. Such a model would discriminate between the two hypotheses raised in Section 4.4 (default-tier under-loading versus claims-history dynamics) more rigorously than the present cross-sectional decomposition permits.
External benchmarking. Comparing the observed loss ratios and segment patterns against published Spanish motor market benchmarks would clarify whether the findings are portfolio-specific or generalisable.
Missingness mechanism. The 1,800 records dropped via listwise deletion show slightly higher premium and claim rate than the retained population. Future work could apply multiple imputation or model the missingness explicitly to test whether the findings are robust to alternative treatments.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
6.3 Methodological reflection
The exercise demonstrates that visual analytics serves three distinct functions in a portfolio review. The first is descriptive, characterising the shape and concentration of the variables that constitute the book. The second is diagnostic, surfacing the segments where premium and exposure are out of balance. The third is communicative, presenting findings in a form that supports further investigation. The bonus methods applied in Section 5 illustrate that the most informative approaches sometimes exploit data-structural features (panel observation, concentration of loss, multivariate clustering) rather than summarising marginal distributions.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
Proportional symbol maps (also known as graduate symbol maps) are a class of maps that use the visual variable of size to represent differences in the magnitude of a discrete, abruptly changing phenomenon, e.g. counts of people. Like choropleth maps, you can create classed or unclassed versions of these maps. The classed ones are known as range-graded or graduated symbols, and the unclassed are called proportional symbols, where the area of the symbols are proportional to the values of the attribute being mapped. In this hands-on exercise, you will learn how to create a proportional symbol map showing the number of wins by Singapore Pools’ outlets using an R package called tmap.


By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will acquire the following skills by using appropriate R packages:

To import an aspatial data file into R.
To convert it into simple point feature data frame and at the same time, to assign an appropriate projection reference to the newly create simple point feature data frame.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
Proportional symbol maps (also known as graduate symbol maps) are a class of maps that use the visual variable of size to represent differences in the magnitude of a discrete, abruptly changing phenomenon, e.g. counts of people. Like choropleth maps, you can create classed or unclassed versions of these maps. The classed ones are known as range-graded or graduated symbols, and the unclassed are called proportional symbols, where the area of the symbols are proportional to the values of the attribute being mapped. In this hands-on exercise, you will learn how to create a proportional symbol map showing the number of wins by Singapore Pools’ outlets using an R package called tmap.


By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will acquire the following skills by using appropriate R packages:

To import an aspatial data file into R.
To convert it into simple point feature data frame and at the same time, to assign an appropriate projection reference to the newly create simple point feature data frame.
To plot interactive proportional symbol maps.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
section: 2.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map
text:
2.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map
The code chunks below are used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
           size = 1,
           col = "black",
           lwd = 1)






2.1.1 Lets make it proportional
To draw a proportional symbol map, we need to assign a numerical variable to the size visual attribute. The code chunks below show that the variable Gp1Gp2Winnings is assigned to size visual attribute.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(use.WebGL = FALSE)








2.1.2 Lets give it a different colour
The proportional symbol map can be further improved by using the colour visual attribute. In the code chunks below, OUTLET_TYPE variable is used as the colour attribute variable.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)









2.1.3 I have a twin brother!! :)
An impressive and little-know feature of tmap’s view mode is that it also works with faceted plots. The argument sync in tm_facets() can be used in this case to produce multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan settings.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) + 
  tm_facets(by= "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)
















Before you end the session, it is wiser to switch tmap’s Viewer back to plot mode by using the code chunk below.

tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
2.2 Extra Alternative

2.2.1 Extra Alternative 3: Surfacing the outlets a proportional map hides

tmap_mode("view")

winners <- sgpools_sf %>% filter(`Gp1Gp2 Winnings` > 0)
zeros   <- sgpools_sf %>% filter(`Gp1Gp2 Winnings` == 0)

tm_shape(winners) +
  tm_bubbles(size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_shape(zeros) +
  tm_bubbles(size = 0.3,
             fill = "grey70",
             col = "grey30",
             lwd = 0.8) +
  tm_view(use.WebGL = FALSE)







The chapter scales each bubble’s area to its winnings, which is precise for high performers but has a hidden cost: an outlet that won nothing has zero area and disappears from the map entirely. This alternative splits the data into outlets with winnings and outlets with none, keeps the proportional coloured bubbles for the former, and redraws the zeros as small fixed grey markers layered on top. Restoring the non-performing outlets makes it immediately clear where Singapore Pools has presence but no Group 1 or 2 wins, a pattern the proportional symbol map erases by construction.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8 - Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
By the end of this hands-on exercise you will be able create the followings data visualisation by using R packages:

plotting a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions,
plotting a cycle plot by using ggplot2 function,
plotting a slopegraph
plotting a horizon chart







Write a code chunk to check, install and launch the following R packages: scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes, gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table and tidyverse.

pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)




In this section, you will learn how to plot a calender heatmap programmatically by using ggplot2 package.
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,
to write function using R programming,
to derive specific date and time related field by using base R and lubridate packages
to perform data preparation task by using tidyr and dplyr packages.



For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, eventlog.csv file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.



First, you will use the code chunk below to import eventlog.csv file into R environment and called the data frame as attacks.

attacks <- read_csv("Data/eventlog.csv")




It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.
For example, kable() can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.

kable(head(attacks))

source_country

There are three columns, namely timestamp, source_country and tz.

timestamp field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.
source_country field stores the source of the attack. It is in ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.
tz field stores time zone of the source IP address.




Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields
Before we can plot the calender heatmap, two new fields namely wkday and hour need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
  }







Note




ymd_hms() and hour() are from lubridate package, and
weekdays() is a base R function.



Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame

wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))







Note



Beside extracting the necessary data into attacks data frame, mutate() of dplyr package is used to convert wkday and hour fields into factor so they’ll be ordered when plotting


Table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.
